topic.title: Sliding Window
topic.summary: Move a contiguous window across an array or string and update its state in O(1) as elements enter and leave — the standard way to turn "check every subarray" into one O(n) pass.
topic.overview:
A **sliding window** is a contiguous range `[left, right]` that moves across an array or string. Instead of recomputing every subarray from scratch (O(n²) or worse), you **update** the window's state when one element enters on the right and one leaves on the left — usually O(1) work — so the whole scan is O(n).

### Two kinds of windows
1. **Fixed size k** — slide by adding `nums[right]` and removing `nums[right − k]`: maximum sum of k elements, Permutation in String, Sliding Window Maximum.
2. **Variable size** — `right` advances every step; `left` moves only when needed:
   - *longest valid window* — expand, **while invalid** shrink, then record (Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, Character Replacement);
   - *shortest valid window* — expand, **while valid** record and shrink (Minimum Size Subarray Sum, Minimum Window Substring).

### What the window remembers
A running sum, a map of counts, a "last seen index" map, a `missing` counter, or a monotonic deque. Picking state whose add/remove are O(1) is the whole trick.

### Recognising it
"Contiguous subarray / substring" plus "longest / shortest / maximum / contains all / at most k" is the classic signal. Shrinking only works when validity is **monotonic** — for example sums of positive numbers. With negative numbers, switch to prefix sums.

### What interviewers listen for
- Why each index enters and leaves the window at most once (the O(n) argument).
- The exact validity condition, and whether you record the answer before or after shrinking.
- Edge cases: k equal to the length, empty strings, no valid window (return 0 or "").

### How to study this topic
Start with the fixed window (Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K), then Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (the simplest variable window), then the "longest" family, then the "shortest" family, and finish with the monotonic deque.

cheatsheet.title: Signals
points: Longest / shortest / max / min over windows
"At most k" distinct letters, replacements or zeros
Contains all characters of another string

cheatsheet.title: Fixed window (size k)
points: Build the first k elements once
Each slide: add nums[right], remove nums[right − k]

cheatsheet.title: Variable window
points: right always moves forward; left only moves forward
Longest: while invalid → shrink, then record
Shortest: while valid → record, then shrink
Each index enters and leaves once → O(n)

cheatsheet.title: Window state
points: Count map + a missing counter for "contains all"
char → last index map for "no repeats" (left jumps)
Monotonic deque of indices for window max / min

cheatsheet.title: Traps
points: Shrinking with negative numbers — the sum is not monotonic
Using a stale lastSeen index that is left of `left`
Array.shift() in JavaScript is O(n) — keep a head index

patterns.name: Fixed-size window
patterns.whenToUse: Every window has exactly k elements: max/min/average of k, anagram windows.

patterns.name: Longest valid window
patterns.whenToUse: Maximise the length while a condition holds (no repeats, at most k changes, at most k distinct).

patterns.name: Shortest valid window
patterns.whenToUse: Minimise the length while a condition holds (sum ≥ target with positives, covers all of t).

patterns.name: Monotonic deque
patterns.whenToUse: Maximum or minimum of every window of size k in O(n).

questions.title: Maximum Sum Subarray of Size K
questions.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **largest sum** of any contiguous subarray of exactly `k` elements.

Values can be negative.

examples.explanation: Every window is negative; the best is -4 + -2.

hints: Brute force re-sums each of the n − k + 1 windows. What work is repeated between two neighbouring windows?
Neighbouring windows share k − 1 elements: only one element enters and one leaves.
Sum the first k once; then for each new right end do `sum += nums[right] − nums[right − k]` and track the maximum.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Re-sum every window of length k.

approaches.name: Prefix sums
approaches.idea: `prefix[i]` = sum of the first i values; a window sum is `prefix[r + 1] − prefix[r + 1 − k]`.

approaches.name: Sliding window
approaches.idea: Keep a running sum; add the element that enters, subtract the one that leaves.

solution.summary: Sum the first k elements once, then slide one step at a time: add the element that enters on the right and subtract the one that leaves on the left, keeping the best sum. Each slide is O(1), so it is O(n) time and O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Why brute force wastes work.** Windows `[i, i+k−1]` and `[i+1, i+k]` share k − 1 elements. Re-adding them costs O(k) per window — O(n·k) overall.

**Sliding the window**
1. `windowSum = nums[0] + … + nums[k−1]`, `best = windowSum`.
2. For `right = k … n−1`: the window gains `nums[right]` and loses `nums[right − k]`, so `windowSum += nums[right] − nums[right − k]`; update `best`.
3. Return `best`.

**Why start best at the first window, not 0?** Values can be negative. If every window sums below zero (e.g. `[-4, -2, -7]`, k = 2 → −6), starting from 0 would return a sum that no window has.

**Complexity.** One pass with O(1) work per slide: O(n) time, O(1) space.

This is the template for every **fixed-size** window: build the first window, then "add `right`, remove `right − k`". Only the state changes — a sum here, letter counts in *Permutation in String*, a deque in *Sliding Window Maximum*.

code.code:
def max_sum_subarray(nums, k):
    window_sum = sum(nums[:k])  # first window
    best = window_sum
    for right in range(k, len(nums)):
        window_sum += nums[right] - nums[right - k]  # add the new, drop the oldest
        best = max(best, window_sum)
    return best

complexity.time: O(n) — one O(1) update per slide

keyPoints: Neighbouring windows share k − 1 elements — update instead of recomputing
`windowSum += nums[right] − nums[right − k]`
Initialise best with the first window because values can be negative
O(n) time, O(1) space versus O(n·k) brute force

visuals.title: Fixed window of size 3 on nums = [3, -1, 4, 1, 5, -9, 2, 6]
visuals.caption: The band is the current window. Each slide adds the highlighted cell on the right and drops the red cell on the left.

steps.note: Build the first window nums[0..2]: 3 + (-1) + 4 = 6. It is the only window summed from scratch; `best = 6`.
Slide right: add nums[3] = 1, drop nums[0] = 3 → 6 + 1 − 3 = 4. best stays 6.
Slide right: add nums[4] = 5, drop nums[1] = -1 → 4 + 5 − (-1) = 10. **New best 10.**
Slide right: add nums[5] = -9, drop nums[2] = 4 → 10 + (-9) − 4 = -3. best stays 10.
Slide right: add nums[6] = 2, drop nums[3] = 1 → -3 + 2 − 1 = -2. best stays 10.
Slide right: add nums[7] = 6, drop nums[4] = 5 → -2 + 6 − 5 = -1. best stays 10.
All 6 windows checked with 2 operations per slide instead of re-adding 3 numbers. Answer **10** from nums[2..4].

visuals.title: Re-summing vs prefix sums vs sliding
rows: Elements touched on the example (n = 8, k = 3)
One pass over all windows of size k

pitfalls: Starting `best` at 0, which is wrong when every window is negative
Off-by-one: the leaving element is `nums[right − k]`, not `nums[right − k + 1]`
Re-summing with `slice` + `reduce` inside the loop — still O(n·k)

followUps.question: What if you need the maximum average instead?
followUps.answer: Use the same window and divide the best sum by k at the end; keep integer sums inside the loop to avoid floating-point drift.

followUps.question: What if the size is not fixed — the longest subarray with sum ≤ S, all values positive?
followUps.answer: Use a variable window: expand right, and while the sum exceeds S move left forward; record right − left + 1. O(n).

questions.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
questions.prompt:
`prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day i. You may buy **once** and sell **once**, and the sale must happen on a later day than the purchase.

Return the maximum profit you can make. If no profit is possible, return 0.

examples.explanation: Buy on day 3 (price 1), sell on day 5 (price 8).
Prices only fall, so the best is not to trade.
Buy at 2 and sell at 4 (or buy at 1 and sell at 3).

hints: Fix the selling day. Which buying day is best for it?
The best buying day is simply the cheapest day before the sale.
Scan once, remembering the cheapest day so far (`buy`). If today is cheaper, move `buy` here; otherwise try selling today.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every (buy, sell) pair with buy < sell.

approaches.name: One pass (running minimum)
approaches.idea: Track the cheapest day so far and the best profit from selling today.

solution.summary: I scan the days once and keep the cheapest day so far as my buy day. If today is cheaper it becomes the new buy day; otherwise I compute the profit of selling today and keep the maximum. O(n) time, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Key observation.** If you sell on day `sell`, the best purchase is the **minimum price before it**. So you only need a running minimum, not every pair.

**As a window.** Let the window be `[buy, sell]`, where `buy` is the cheapest day seen so far.
1. `buy = 0`, `best = 0`.
2. For each `sell` from 1 to n − 1:
   - `prices[sell] < prices[buy]` → a cheaper day; every later sale earns more from here, so restart the window: `buy = sell`;
   - otherwise → profit `prices[sell] − prices[buy]`; update `best`.
3. Return `best` (0 when prices only fall).

**Why moving buy forward never loses the answer.** Once a cheaper day appears, any later sale makes more money buying on that day, so the older buy days are useless from then on.

**Complexity.** One pass: O(n) time, O(1) space. (Same idea as Kadane's algorithm on the day-to-day price differences.)
keyPoints: For each selling day, the best buying day is the minimum price before it
Track the running minimum (buy) and the best profit in one pass
Return 0 when prices only fall — never a negative profit
O(n) time and O(1) space versus O(n²) for all pairs

visuals.title: One pass over prices = [7, 2, 6, 1, 4, 8, 3]
visuals.caption: `buy` (yellow) is the cheapest day so far; the band is the trade buy → sell being evaluated. Grey days can no longer be the best buy day.

steps.note: Day 0 is the cheapest day seen so far, so `buy = 0`. The window [buy, sell] is "bought on buy, selling on sell".
prices[1] = 2 < prices[buy] = 7: a cheaper day. Any future sale is better from here, so restart the window: `buy = 1`.
Sell on day 2: 6 − 2 = 4. **New best 4.**
prices[3] = 1 < prices[buy] = 2: a cheaper day. Any future sale is better from here, so restart the window: `buy = 3`.
Sell on day 4: 4 − 1 = 3. best stays 4.
Sell on day 5: 8 − 1 = 7. **New best 7.**
Sell on day 6: 3 − 1 = 2. best stays 7.
Done in one pass: buy on day 3 at 1, sell on day 5 at 8 → max profit **7**.

visuals.title: All pairs vs one pass
rows: For every buy day, try every later sell day
Keep the cheapest day so far; try selling today
Pairs examined on the example (7 days)

pitfalls: Returning max(prices) − min(prices) — the minimum may come after the maximum
Allowing a sale on or before the buying day
Returning a negative number when no profit is possible

followUps.question: What if you may make unlimited transactions (holding one share at a time)?
followUps.answer: Add up every positive day-to-day increase: the sum of max(0, prices[i] − prices[i − 1]). O(n).

followUps.question: What if there is a transaction fee or a cooldown day?
followUps.answer: Use DP with two states per day — holding a share or not — and put the fee or cooldown into the transitions. O(n) time, O(1) space.

questions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
questions.prompt: Given a string `s`, return the length of the **longest substring** (contiguous) in which no character appears more than once.
constraints: `s` may contain letters, digits, symbols and spaces
hints: Checking every substring is O(n²) or worse. Can a window that grows on the right and shrinks on the left do it in one pass?
When the new character is already inside the window, everything up to and including its previous copy has to leave.
Store each character's last index in a map. If `lastSeen[c] ≥ left`, jump `left` to `lastSeen[c] + 1`. The answer is the largest `right − left + 1`.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Check every substring for repeated characters.

approaches.name: Window + set
approaches.idea: Grow right; while s[right] is already in the set, remove s[left] and move left.

approaches.name: Window + last-index map
approaches.idea: Jump left directly past the previous copy of the repeated character.

solution.summary: I keep a window with no repeated characters and a map from each character to its last index. For each new character, if its last index is inside the window I jump `left` just past it; then the window is valid again and I record its length. Each character is processed once: O(n) time.
solution.explanation:
**Window invariant.** `s[left..right]` never contains a repeated character.

**Algorithm**
1. `lastSeen` = empty map, `left = 0`, `best = 0`.
2. For each `right`, with `c = s[right]`:
   - if `c` was last seen at index `j ≥ left` (inside the window), set `left = j + 1` — the old copy and everything before it must leave;
   - `lastSeen[c] = right`;
   - `best = max(best, right − left + 1)`.
3. Return `best`.

**Why the `≥ left` check matters.** The map remembers indices from long ago. In "abcbdca" the last 'a' was seen at index 0 while `left` is already 3 — that 'a' is not in the window, so `left` must stay. Without the check, `left` would jump *backwards* (try "abba").

**Set version.** With a set you shrink one step at a time: `while (set.has(c)) set.delete(s[left++])`. It is also O(n) because each index enters and leaves once; the map version simply jumps.

**Complexity.** O(n) time; O(min(n, alphabet size)) space for the map.

complexity.time: O(n) — each character is processed once and left only moves forward
complexity.space: O(min(n, alphabet size)) for the map

keyPoints: Variable window: right always advances, left only moves forward
A char → last index map lets left jump instead of crawling
Only jump when the previous index is ≥ left (inside the window)
Answer = max of right − left + 1; O(n) time

visuals.title: Last-index map on s = "abcbdca"
visuals.caption: The band is the window s[left..right]. Red cells are dropped when left jumps; the map holds the last index of each character.

steps.note: Empty map, `left = 0`, `best = 0`. The window `s[left..right]` will always contain distinct characters.
'a' is new. Window "a" has length 1 → **best = 1**.
'b' is new. Window "ab" has length 2 → **best = 2**.
'c' is new. Window "abc" has length 3 → **best = 3**.
'b' was last seen at index 1, inside the window → jump `left` to 2, past the old copy. Window "cb" has length 2 (best 3).
'd' is new. Window "cbd" has length 3 (best 3).
'c' was last seen at index 2, inside the window → jump `left` to 3, past the old copy. Window "bdc" has length 3 (best 3).
'a' was seen at index 0, but that is left of `left` (3) — outside the window, so it does not count. Window "bdca" has length 4 → **best = 4**.
Each index entered the window once and `left` only moved forward → O(n). Longest substring without repeats: "bdca", length **4**.

visuals.title: Three ways to keep the window repeat-free
rows: While s[right] is in the set, remove s[left] and move left
left = lastSeen[c] + 1 when that copy is inside the window
O(n) — each index enters and leaves once
Adding the char before removing the old copy
Jumping left backwards to a stale index

pitfalls: Ignoring the `lastSeen[c] ≥ left` check, so left moves backwards (e.g. "abba" would give 3 instead of 2)
Setting `left = lastSeen[c]` instead of `lastSeen[c] + 1`
Treating it as a subsequence problem — the characters must be contiguous

followUps.question: How do you return the substring itself?
followUps.answer: Store the start index whenever best improves and slice once at the end.

followUps.question: What about the longest substring with at most k distinct characters?
followUps.answer: Keep a count map; after adding s[right], while the map has more than k keys, decrement s[left] (delete it at zero) and move left. O(n).

questions.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
questions.prompt:
You are given a string `s` of uppercase English letters and an integer `k`. You may change **at most k** characters into any other uppercase letter.

Return the length of the longest substring that can be made of a single repeated letter.
hints: For one fixed window, how many replacements does it need to become a single letter?
It needs `length − (count of its most frequent letter)` replacements.
Grow the window; while `length − maxFreq > k`, shrink from the left. Track the largest valid length. You never need to decrease maxFreq.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: For every substring, count letters and check length − maxCount ≤ k.

approaches.name: Window, recompute the max
approaches.idea: Variable window; recompute the top count over 26 letters when checking validity.

approaches.name: Window, historical maxFreq
approaches.idea: Keep the largest count ever seen; the window only has to beat the best length so far.

solution.summary: A window can become one letter if its length minus the count of its most frequent letter is at most k. I grow the window to the right, shrink from the left while that fails, and record the largest valid length. Keeping maxFreq as the best count seen so far makes it O(n).
solution.explanation:
**Validity.** A window needs `length − maxFreq` replacements, where `maxFreq` is the count of its most common letter (keep that letter, replace the rest). It is valid when `length − maxFreq ≤ k`.

**Algorithm**
1. `count` map, `left = 0`, `maxFreq = 0`, `best = 0`.
2. For each `right`: add `s[right]` to `count`; `maxFreq = max(maxFreq, count[s[right]])`.
3. While `right − left + 1 − maxFreq > k`: decrement `count[s[left]]`, `left++`.
4. `best = max(best, right − left + 1)`.

**The subtle part: maxFreq never decreases.** After a shrink, the true top count inside the window can be lower than `maxFreq`, so the window may even be invalid for a while. That is harmless: from then on the window has length `maxFreq + k` and just slides at that size. It can only grow when a letter **inside the current window** gets a count above `maxFreq` — and at that moment the window really is valid. So `best` is never overstated. The last steps of the visual show this.

If that argument feels risky in an interview, recompute the max over the 26 counts in the while condition: O(26·n), still linear.

**Complexity.** O(n) time, O(26) space.

code.code:
def character_replacement(s, k):
    count = {}  # char -> count inside the window
    left = max_freq = best = 0
    for right, c in enumerate(s):
        count[c] = count.get(c, 0) + 1
        max_freq = max(max_freq, count[c])
        while right - left + 1 - max_freq > k:  # too many chars to replace
            count[s[left]] -= 1
            left += 1
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best

complexity.time: O(n) — left and right each move at most n times

keyPoints: Replacements needed = window length − count of the most frequent letter
Variable window: expand right, shrink left while length − maxFreq > k
maxFreq may stay at its historical maximum — the answer is never overstated
O(n) time, O(26) space (O(26·n) if you recompute the max)

visuals.title: Window on s = "BAAACAAB", k = 1
visuals.caption: Blue band = valid window; red band = `length − maxFreq > k`, so the loop shrinks it; yellow band = the check passes only because maxFreq is stale (the window really needs more than k replacements). The map holds letter counts inside the window.

steps.note: k = 1: a window is valid when `length − maxFreq ≤ k` — everything except the most frequent letter gets replaced.
Add 'B' → count 1, maxFreq 1. Length 1 − 1 = 0 ≤ k → valid, **best = 1**.
Add 'A' → count 1, maxFreq 1. Length 2 − 1 = 1 ≤ k → valid, **best = 2**.
Add 'A' → count 2, maxFreq 2. Length 3 − 2 = 1 ≤ k → valid, **best = 3**.
Add 'A' → count 3, maxFreq 3. Length 4 − 3 = 1 ≤ k → valid, **best = 4**.
Add 'C' → length 5, maxFreq 3: 5 − 3 = 2 replacements > k = 1. The window is invalid — shrink from the left.
Drop 'B' and move `left` to 1: length 4, 4 − 3 = 1 ≤ k → valid again. best stays 4.
Add 'A' → count 4, maxFreq 4. Length 5 − 4 = 1 ≤ k → valid, **best = 5**.
Add 'A' → count 5, maxFreq 5. Length 6 − 5 = 1 ≤ k → valid, **best = 6**.
Add 'B' → length 7, maxFreq 5: 7 − 5 = 2 replacements > k = 1. The window is invalid — shrink from the left.

Drop 'A', `left` = 2: length 6 − maxFreq 5 = 1 ≤ k, so the loop stops. Careful: "AACAAB" really has at most 4 of one letter, but `maxFreq` stays 5 on purpose. The window now just slides at length 6 = best and can only grow once a letter's count beats 5 — so best is never overstated.
Answer **6**: "AAACAA" becomes "AAAAAA" with 1 replacement.

visuals.title: Recompute the max vs keep the historical max
rows: length − maxFreq > k, maxFreq never decreases
No — it can be briefly invalid, but never longer than the best answer
Needs the "answer is never overstated" argument

pitfalls: Recomputing the most frequent letter by scanning the whole window each step (O(n²))
Using the count of `s[right]` instead of the window's most frequent letter
Decrementing maxFreq on a shrink without recomputing it — it can become too small and shrink valid windows

followUps.question: What if the string can contain any characters?
followUps.answer: Use a hash map for counts; the algorithm does not change (space becomes O(distinct characters)).

followUps.question: Longest run of 1s if you may flip at most k zeros?
followUps.answer: Same window: count zeros inside it; while zeros > k, move left. It is this problem with a two-letter alphabet.

questions.title: Permutation in String
questions.prompt: Given two strings `s1` and `s2` of lowercase English letters, return `true` if some **contiguous substring of `s2`** is a permutation (rearrangement) of `s1`, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: "a" and "b" are never next to each other.

constraints: Both strings contain lowercase English letters only
hints: A permutation of s1 has exactly the same length and the same letter counts as s1.
So only windows of length len(s1) matter — a fixed-size window.
Keep `need[c]` = (count in s1) − (count in window) and a counter `missing` of uncovered letters. Add the entering letter, remove the leaving one; return true as soon as missing hits 0.

approaches.name: Generate permutations
approaches.idea: Generate every permutation of s1 and search for each in s2.

approaches.name: Sort each window
approaches.idea: Compare sorted(window) with sorted(s1).

approaches.name: Compare count arrays
approaches.idea: Slide a 26-slot count array and compare it with s1's counts.

approaches.name: Missing counter
approaches.idea: Track how many needed letters are uncovered; O(1) per slide.

solution.summary: A permutation has the same letter counts, so I slide a window of length len(s1) over s2 and track how many letters of s1 are still missing from it. Adding or removing a letter updates that counter in O(1), and when it reaches 0 the window is a permutation. O(n) time, O(26) space.
solution.explanation:
**Reduce the question.** "Some substring is a permutation of s1" ⇔ "some window of length m = |s1| has the same letter counts as s1". Order inside the window does not matter.

**State**
- `need[c]` = (count of c in s1) − (count of c in the window). Positive → still needed; negative → surplus.
- `missing` = the sum of the positive `need` values = letters of s1 not covered yet.

**Algorithm**
1. Fill `need` from s1; `missing = m`.
2. For each `right`:
   - entering `c = s2[right]`: if `need[c] > 0`, `missing--`; then `need[c]--`;
   - once the window is full, the leaving letter `s2[right − m]`: `need[out]++`; if it became `> 0` we lost a needed letter → `missing++`;
   - `missing == 0` → return `true`.
3. Return `false`.

**Why missing == 0 is enough.** The window has exactly m letters, and `missing == 0` means all m letters of s1 are covered — there is no room left for anything else, so the counts match exactly.

**Complexity.** O(1) per slide → O(n) time (n = |s2|), O(26) space.
keyPoints: Permutation ⇔ same length and same letter counts
Fixed-size window of length len(s1)
need[c] plus a missing counter give O(1) updates per slide
Same counting trick as Minimum Window Substring
O(n) time, O(26) space

visuals.title: Fixed window of size 3: s1 = "abc", s2 = "cbxacbd"
visuals.caption: The band is the window over s2. `need` holds what s1 still needs (negative = surplus); `missing` counts uncovered letters.

steps.note: Count what s1 needs: a:1, b:1, c:1. `missing = 3` characters are not yet covered. The window over s2 has fixed size 3.
Add 'c': it was needed → missing = 2. Window "c" is still filling up.
Add 'b': it was needed → missing = 1. Window "cb" is still filling up.
Add 'x': not needed (need[x] becomes -1, a surplus) → missing stays 1. Window "cbx" still misses 1 → not a permutation.
Add 'a': it was needed → missing = 0; drop 'c': we lose a needed char → missing 1. Window "bxa" still misses 1 → not a permutation.
Add 'c': it was needed → missing = 0; drop 'b': we lose a needed char → missing 1. Window "xac" still misses 1 → not a permutation.
Add 'b': it was needed → missing = 0; drop 'x': s1 has no 'x', so it was surplus → missing stays 0. Window "acb" has missing = 0 → it is a permutation of "abc" → **return true**.

rows: Find All Anagrams, Minimum Window Substring
Too slow when s1 is long
Comparing arrays with == instead of Arrays.equals
Checking need[c] after decrementing instead of before

pitfalls: Using a variable-size window — it must be exactly len(s1) long
Comparing two count arrays with `==` (a reference comparison in Java and JavaScript)
Forgetting the early `false` when s1 is longer than s2

followUps.question: Return every start index of an anagram of s1 in s2 (Find All Anagrams)?
followUps.answer: Same window; instead of returning true, record right − m + 1 whenever missing == 0. O(n).

followUps.question: What if the strings can contain any Unicode characters?
followUps.answer: Use a hash map for need instead of a 26-slot array; nothing else changes.

questions.title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
questions.prompt: Given an array of **positive** integers `nums` and a positive integer `target`, return the length of the **shortest** contiguous subarray whose sum is at least `target`. If there is none, return 0.

examples.explanation: Even the whole array sums to only 6.

hints: All numbers are positive. What happens to a subarray's sum when you add an element on the right or remove one on the left?
Adding grows the sum and removing shrinks it — so for each right end, move the left end forward as long as the sum stays ≥ target.
Expand `right` and add to `sum`; while `sum ≥ target`, record `right − left + 1`, subtract `nums[left]` and move `left`.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: For each start, extend until the sum reaches target.

approaches.name: Prefix sums + binary search
approaches.idea: Prefix sums are increasing (positive values), so for each start binary-search the first end that reaches target.

approaches.name: Sliding window
approaches.idea: Expand right; while the sum is ≥ target, record the length and shrink from the left.

solution.summary: Because every number is positive, growing the window increases the sum and shrinking decreases it. I expand the right end, and whenever the sum reaches the target I record the length and shrink from the left until it drops below. Each index enters and leaves once: O(n) time, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Monotonicity is the key.** With positive numbers, extending a window increases its sum and removing from the left decreases it. Once `[left, right]` reaches the target, any longer window with the same `right` is worse — so move `left` forward.

**Algorithm ("shortest valid window" template)**
1. `left = 0`, `sum = 0`, `best = ∞`.
2. For each `right`: `sum += nums[right]`.
3. While `sum ≥ target`: `best = min(best, right − left + 1)`, then `sum −= nums[left]`, `left++`.
4. Return `best`, or 0 if it is still ∞.

Note **where** the answer is recorded: inside the while loop, while the window is valid. The "longest valid window" template is the mirror image: shrink while invalid, then record after the loop.

**Complexity.** `left` and `right` each move at most n times → O(n) time, O(1) space.

**When it breaks.** With negative numbers the sum is no longer monotonic and shrinking can miss the answer (target 3, nums [1, −1, 3] would report 3 instead of 1). Then you need prefix sums with a monotonic deque — a good follow-up to mention.

code.code:
def min_sub_array_len(target, nums):
    left = total = 0
    best = float("inf")
    for right, x in enumerate(nums):
        total += x  # expand
        while total >= target:  # valid: record it, then try to shrink
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            total -= nums[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float("inf") else best

complexity.time: O(n) — left and right each move at most n times

keyPoints: Positive numbers make the window sum monotonic — that is what allows shrinking
Shortest-window template: while valid → record, then shrink
Each index enters and leaves once → O(n)
Return 0 when no window reaches the target

Every index entered and left the window at most once → O(n). Shortest window with sum ≥ 10: nums[4..5] = [6, 5], length **2**.

followUps.question: What if the array may contain negative numbers?
followUps.answer: The window no longer works. Use prefix sums and a deque of indices with increasing prefix values: for each end, pop from the front while prefix[end] − prefix[front] ≥ target (recording lengths). O(n).

followUps.question: Can you solve it in O(n log n) another way?
followUps.answer: Prefix sums are strictly increasing for positive numbers, so for each start you can binary-search the first end whose prefix difference reaches target.

questions.title: Minimum Window Substring
questions.prompt:
Given strings `s` and `t`, return the **shortest substring of `s`** that contains every character of `t` **including duplicates** (if `t` has two "A"s, the window needs at least two "A"s). If no such substring exists, return the empty string `""`.

If several shortest windows exist, return the leftmost one.

examples.explanation: "CADB" also contains A, B and C, but "BAC" (indices 3–5) is shorter.
The window needs two "A"s and a "B".

hints: This is the "shortest valid window" pattern: grow until the window contains t, then shrink while it still does.
How can you check "contains all of t" in O(1) after each move? Keep counts of what is still needed.
`need[c]` = copies still needed (negative = surplus); `missing` = characters of t not covered. Expand right; while missing == 0, record the window, then remove s[left] and move left.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Check every substring against t's character counts.

approaches.name: Window, compare full counts
approaches.idea: Variable window, but test validity by comparing every character count.

approaches.name: Window with a missing counter
approaches.idea: A need map plus a missing counter make every update O(1).

solution.summary: I use a variable window with a need map and a missing counter. I expand the right end until the window covers every character of t, then shrink from the left while it still covers t, recording the shortest window. Each character enters and leaves once: O(|s| + |t|) time.
solution.explanation:
**State** (σ = alphabet size)
- `need[c]` = how many more copies of c the window needs. It starts as t's counts and goes **negative** for surplus copies or characters t does not use.
- `missing` = number of characters of t still uncovered (the sum of the positive `need` values).

**Algorithm (shortest valid window)**
1. Build `need` from t; `missing = |t|`.
2. For each `right`, with `c = s[right]`: if `need[c] > 0` then `missing--`; then `need[c]--`.
3. While `missing == 0` (the window covers t):
   - record it if it is shorter than the best;
   - remove `s[left]`: `need[s[left]]++`; if that makes it `> 0`, a needed character is gone → `missing++`;
   - `left++`.
4. Return the best window, or "".

**Why shrinking is safe.** Removing a character that t does not use, or a surplus copy, leaves its `need ≤ 0`, so the window still covers t and just got shorter. The first removal of a character that t really needs makes `missing = 1` and stops the loop — the window just before it was the shortest valid one ending at `right`.

**Complexity.** `left` and `right` each move at most |s| times, plus O(|t|) to build `need`: **O(|s| + |t|)** time and O(σ) space.

It is the same counter trick as *Permutation in String*; the difference is that this window has a variable size and may hold surplus characters.

complexity.time: O(|s| + |t|) — each index of s enters and leaves the window once

keyPoints: Shortest-valid-window template: expand until valid, then shrink while valid
need map with negative values for surplus + a missing counter → O(1) validity check
Duplicates in t are handled by counts, not by a set
O(|s| + |t|) time, O(alphabet) space
Store bestStart and bestLen; slice once at the end

Add 'A': it was needed → missing = 1.
Add 'D': not in t (need[D] = -1); missing stays 1.
Add 'B': it was needed → missing = 0. **The window covers t** — record it and shrink.
"CADB" (length 4) covers t → **best = "CADB"**. Drop 'C': need[C] = 1 > 0 → we lost a needed char, missing = 1; stop shrinking.
Add 'A': already covered, so need[A] drops to -1 (a surplus copy); missing stays 1.
Add 'C': it was needed → missing = 0. **The window covers t** — record it and shrink.
"ADBAC" (length 5) covers t, but is not shorter than the best (4). Drop 'A': it was a surplus copy (need[A] = 0), so the window still covers t — keep shrinking.
"DBAC" (length 4) covers t, but is not shorter than the best (4). Drop 'D': 'D' is not in t, so the window still covers t — keep shrinking.
"BAC" (length 3) covers t → **best = "BAC"**. Drop 'B': need[B] = 1 > 0 → we lost a needed char, missing = 1; stop shrinking.
Add 'E': not in t (need[E] = -1); missing stays 1.
Add 'B': it was needed → missing = 0. **The window covers t** — record it and shrink.
"ACEB" (length 4) covers t, but is not shorter than the best (3). Drop 'A': need[A] = 1 > 0 → we lost a needed char, missing = 1; stop shrinking.
`right` reached the end. Smallest window containing every char of "ABC": **"BAC"** (index 3..5).

visuals.title: Same counter, two kinds of window
rows: Moves in lockstep with right (index right − m leaves)
Moves only while the window stays valid

pitfalls: Using a set for t, which ignores duplicates such as t = "AAB"
Comparing full count maps on every move (O(σ) each) when a missing counter is O(1)
Slicing the substring inside the loop — an extra O(n) copy each time
Forgetting to return "" when no window exists

followUps.question: Why is it O(n) even with a while loop inside the for loop?
followUps.answer: `left` only moves forward and never passes `right`, so over the whole run the inner loop executes at most |s| times in total.

followUps.question: Another way to track validity?
followUps.answer: Count `formed` = number of distinct characters whose required count is met, and compare it with the number of distinct characters in t. It is equivalent to the missing counter.

questions.title: Sliding Window Maximum
questions.prompt:
Given an integer array `nums` and a window size `k`, a window of size k slides from the left end of the array to the right end, one position at a time.

Return an array with the **maximum of each window** (n − k + 1 values).
hints: Recomputing each window's max is O(k) per window. Which elements can never be a window maximum again?
If a newer element is at least as big as an older one, the older one is useless for every future window.
Keep a deque of indices with decreasing values. For each i: drop the front if it left the window, pop smaller values from the back, push i; the front is the maximum.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Scan each window for its maximum.

approaches.name: Max-heap with lazy deletion
approaches.idea: Push (value, index); pop the top while its index is outside the window.

approaches.name: Monotonic deque
approaches.idea: Indices with decreasing values; each index is pushed and popped at most once.

solution.summary: I keep a deque of indices whose values decrease from front to back. For each new element I drop the front if it slid out of the window, pop every smaller value from the back because it can never be a maximum again, and push the new index; the front is then the window maximum. Each index is pushed and popped at most once: O(n).
solution.explanation:
**Which elements matter?** If `j < i` and `nums[j] ≤ nums[i]`, then `nums[j]` is never needed as the maximum of a window that also contains `i` (`nums[i]` is at least as big) — and `j` leaves the window before `i` does. So `j` can be thrown away for good.

**Deque invariant.** The deque holds indices from the current window whose values **strictly decrease** from front to back, so the front is the maximum.

**Algorithm.** For each index `i`:
1. If the front index is `≤ i − k`, it has left the window → remove it from the front.
2. While the value at the back is `≤ nums[i]` → pop it (it is dominated by `nums[i]`).
3. Push `i` at the back.
4. Once `i ≥ k − 1` the window is full → append `nums[front]` to the result.

**Complexity.** Every index is pushed once and popped at most once (from the front or the back), so the total work is **O(n)** even though there is a loop inside the loop. The live deque holds at most k indices → O(k) extra space. (In the JavaScript version the expired slots before `head` stay in the array, so it can grow to n entries — O(n) memory, the same order as the output. Use a ring buffer of size k if that matters.)

**Implementation notes.** Store **indices**, not values — you need them to know when the front leaves the window. In JavaScript, `Array.prototype.shift()` is O(n), so the solution keeps a `head` index instead; Java has `ArrayDeque` and Python `collections.deque`.

complexity.time: O(n) amortised — each index is pushed and popped at most once
complexity.space: O(k) for the live deque in Python/Java; the JavaScript head-index array also keeps expired slots, so it can reach n entries (O(n), the same order as the output)

keyPoints: Smaller, older elements are dominated and can be discarded forever
Deque of indices with decreasing values; the front is the max
Expire the front when its index ≤ i − k
Amortised O(n): each index is pushed and popped at most once
Mention the O(n log n) heap alternative

visuals.title: Monotonic deque on nums = [2, 7, 3, 1, 5, 2, 6, 4], k = 3
visuals.caption: The band is the window. Deque members are yellow and the front (window max) green; red = popped from the back, grey = expired from the front.

steps.note: k = 3. The deque stores **indices** whose values decrease from front to back, so the front is always the window maximum.
i = 0: push index 0 (value 2). The window is not full yet.
i = 1: pop 2 @0 from the back — it is ≤ 7 and older, so it can never be a maximum again; push index 1 (value 7). The window is not full yet.
i = 2: push index 2 (value 3). The window [0..2] is full → its max is the front, **7**.
i = 3: push index 3 (value 1). The window [1..3] is full → its max is the front, **7**.

i = 4: index 1 (value 7) slid out of the window → drop it from the front; pop 1 @3 and 3 @2 from the back — they are ≤ 5 and older, so they can never be a maximum again; push index 4 (value 5). The window [2..4] is full → its max is the front, **5**.
i = 5: push index 5 (value 2). The window [3..5] is full → its max is the front, **5**.
i = 6: pop 2 @5 and 5 @4 from the back — they are ≤ 6 and older, so they can never be a maximum again; push index 6 (value 6). The window [4..6] is full → its max is the front, **6**.
i = 7: push index 7 (value 4). The window [5..7] is full → its max is the front, **6**.
Each index was pushed once and popped at most once → O(n) total. Window maxima: [7, 7, 5, 5, 6, 6] — they come from the green elements 7, 5 and 6.

visuals.title: Brute force vs heap vs monotonic deque
rows: Heap of (value, index); discard tops outside the window

pitfalls: Storing values instead of indices, so you cannot tell when the front has left the window
Using `Array.shift()` in JavaScript, which makes each front removal O(n)
Emitting a result before the first window is full (i < k − 1)

followUps.question: How would you get the minimum of each window?
followUps.answer: Keep the deque increasing instead: pop from the back while the back value is ≥ the new value.

followUps.question: Where else does the monotonic deque show up?
followUps.answer: Shortest subarray with sum ≥ K when values can be negative (a deque over prefix sums), and DP optimisations such as "best dp value among the last k positions".

quiz.question: Which problem is the best fit for the sliding window technique?
options: Longest substring with at most 2 distinct characters
Count pairs (i, j) with nums[i] + nums[j] = target in an unsorted array
Longest increasing subsequence
Shortest path between two cells in a grid
quiz.explanation: Sliding windows work on contiguous ranges whose validity changes predictably when you add or remove at the ends. Pairs in an unsorted array call for a hash map, LIS is not contiguous (DP), and shortest paths need BFS.

quiz.question: A fixed-size window of size k moves so that it now ends at index right. How do you update the running sum in O(1)?
options: sum += nums[right]
sum += nums[right] - nums[right - k + 1]
sum = nums[right - k + 1] + … + nums[right] (recompute)
sum += nums[right] - nums[right - k]
quiz.explanation: The new window is [right − k + 1, right], so the element that just left is nums[right − k]. Recomputing is correct but costs O(k) per step.

quiz.question: Why does the shrinking window for "shortest subarray with sum ≥ target" fail when the array contains negative numbers?
options: Negative numbers overflow the running sum
The window can grow larger than the array
It does not fail — the same code still works
The sum is no longer monotonic: dropping an element can make it bigger, so shorter valid subarrays are missed
quiz.explanation: Example: target = 3, nums = [1, −1, 3]. The window reaches sum 3 at length 3, drops the 1 (sum becomes 2) and stops, reporting 3 — but [3] alone has length 1. Use prefix sums with a monotonic deque instead.

quiz.question: In Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (last-index map), why check `lastSeen.get(c) >= left` before moving left?
options: The map can hold an index from before the window; jumping to it would move left backwards
To skip characters that are not letters
To avoid an exception when the key is missing
Because only characters at even indices matter
quiz.explanation: Old indices stay in the map. For "abba", the final "a" was seen at index 0 while left is already 2; without the check left would jump back to 1 and the answer would be 3 instead of 2.

quiz.question: What is the time complexity of a variable-size sliding window in which left and right only ever move forward?
options: O(n²) because of the nested while loop
O(n log n)
O(n) — each index enters and leaves the window at most once
O(n · k)
quiz.explanation: The inner loop can run many times in one iteration, but left moves at most n times over the whole run. Total pointer moves ≤ 2n → O(n) (amortised analysis).

quiz.question: In Sliding Window Maximum, what does the deque store?
options: Indices whose values decrease from front to back
Values in increasing order
All k values of the current window, sorted
Indices of the window in insertion order
quiz.explanation: Indices let you expire the front when it leaves the window; keeping their values decreasing makes the front the maximum. Sorting the whole window would cost O(k log k) per step.

quiz.question: In Longest Repeating Character Replacement, when is a window valid?
options: When it contains at most k distinct letters
When length − (count of its most frequent letter) ≤ k
When its most frequent letter appears at least k times
When its length is at most k
quiz.explanation: Keep the most frequent letter and replace everything else: that needs length − maxFreq changes, which must be ≤ k.

quiz.question: In Permutation in String, how large is the window over s2?
options: It grows until it contains every letter of s1
len(s2) − len(s1)
Exactly len(s1)
It starts at 1 and doubles
quiz.explanation: A permutation of s1 has exactly len(s1) letters, so only windows of that size can match — a fixed-size window.

quiz.question: What does this print?
quiz.explanation: The windows of size 2 sum to 3, 1, 3, −4 and −1, so the best is 3. 6 would be the best sum of a subarray of any length ([4, −1, 2, 1]) — that is a different problem (Kadane's algorithm).

quiz.question: In Minimum Window Substring, need['A'] is −1 for the current window. What does that mean?
options: The window is still missing one "A"
The window holds one more "A" than t requires
"A" does not occur in t
The window is invalid
quiz.explanation: need starts at t's counts and goes down as characters enter. −1 means one surplus "A" — it can be dropped without breaking the window.

quiz.question: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with prices = [3, 8, 1, 5]. What does the one-pass algorithm return?
quiz.explanation: Buy at 3 and sell at 8 for 5. After the price drops to 1, the best is 5 − 1 = 4, which does not beat 5. 7 (8 − 1) is impossible because you cannot sell before you buy.

quiz.question: In the "shortest valid window" template (e.g. Minimum Size Subarray Sum), where do you record the answer?
options: Before adding nums[right]
Inside the while loop, before removing nums[left]
After the while loop has finished
Only when right reaches the end of the array
quiz.explanation: The window is valid only inside the loop; once the loop ends it has just become invalid. The "longest valid window" template is the mirror image: shrink while invalid, then record after the loop.
